brief.head: Four magic terms
brief.text: Say mar­ket fail­ure, pub­lic good, ad­verse se­lec­tion and moral haz­ard cor­rectly, Ajay Shah said, “then ba­si­cally you’re an econ­o­mist”. Every field bor­rows com­mon words for its own mean­ings. {042-C01}

brief.head: Follow the tribe
brief.text: Within eight years, Amit Varma said, Donald Trump turned the Republican Party against much of what it stood for. Many peo­ple, he con­cluded, hold prin­ci­ples only be­cause their tribe does. {042-C10}

brief.head: Hollow parties
brief.text: Parties need to be in­sti­tu­tions too, Ajay Shah ar­gued, not the iron hand of one or two peo­ple. The gut­ting of the Republicans will mat­ter for 25 years. {042-C11}

brief.head: Democracy, plus two
brief.text: People hav­ing power is “a damn good thing”, Amit Varma said. But it also needs a re­pub­lic that pro­tects in­di­vid­ual rights, and a healthy pub­lic dis­course where sim­plis­tic nar­ra­tives lose. {042-C16}

brief.head: Keeping score
brief.text: Rival democ­racy mea­sures dis­agree some­what but agree quite a bit, Ajay Shah said. He reads Freedom House for ease of use; V-Dem, he thinks, is bet­ter but more work. {042-R12}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what populism really means
lead.head: Not popular, just populist

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 42

body: Amit Varma opened the episode hold­ing a leaf, which he in­tro­duced as an an­cient man­u­script bear­ing mys­te­ri­ous words in a mys­te­ri­ous lan­guage. The word the hosts set out to de­code was one ev­ery­body uses: pop­ulism.
“I’m just a clue­less econ­o­mist,” Ajay Shah con­fessed. For years he had thought pop­ulism meant some­thing like pop­u­lar. “And what’s wrong with pop­u­lar?”
Varma had al­ready given the an­swer. Populism is not what is pop­u­lar: in the sense po­lit­i­cal sci­en­tists use it, it is toxic.
Neither host claimed to be an ex­pert. But both, Varma said, have skin in the game, and Shah called 2024 “a re­ally im­por­tant year” in the jour­ney of pop­ulism.
## The check­list
Their guide was Jan-Werner Müller’s *What Is Populism?*, which lists seven things that pop­ulists have in com­mon.
The core claim, Varma said, is that “only some of the peo­ple are the peo­ple”. Populists treat their sup­port­ers as the peo­ple and ev­ery­one else as il­le­git­i­mate. {042-C02}

The rest of the list fol­lows: anti-elite rhetoric, ma­jori­ties that “act like mis­treated mi­nori­ties”, par­ties that turn into per­son­al­ity cults, a show of being one of the peo­ple, sim­plis­tic nar­ra­tives and, grow­ing out of them all, con­spir­acy the­o­ries.
Varma’s favourite of the seven is the sim­plis­tic nar­ra­tive. The world is so com­plex, he said, that “sim­ple sto­ries are a fea­ture, not a bug for the nor­mal per­son”. {042-C05}
Tell un­em­ployed work­ers that their jobs went over­seas and im­mi­grants took the rest, and the story ap­pears to ex­plain the world. It also sup­plies some­one to rail against.
Hatred, Shah added, is a sim­plis­tic nar­ra­tive that ap­peals to emo­tion. “Great lead­ers make us bet­ter than who we are,” he said. Populist lead­ers “bring out the worst in us”.
Varma added a cor­rec­tive for the elites: when peo­ple vote against your val­ues, “some­thing is wrong with you and your mes­sage”.
## Power, and how to keep it
Once pop­ulists win, Varma said, they need “an ad­di­tional play­book” to make sure they don’t lose power: colonise the state, re­ward clients and si­lence civil so­ci­ety. {042-C12}
Shah’s Roman short­hand for the re­sult was bread and cir­cus: hand­outs to pla­cate peo­ple, and a drum­beat of noise to keep them from think­ing.

He then toured four coun­tries he fol­lows. In America, Donald Trump’s own agen­cies re­fused to tor­ment his ri­vals. In Israel, peo­ple from elite mil­i­tary for­ma­tions led protests in de­fence of the judges. Hungary has turned thug­gish de­spite being in the European Union.

Poland was the story of re­demp­tion. After ten years under the Law and Justice Party, the cen­tre-left party led by Donald Tusk won in October 2023. Now it must undo the dam­age with­out break­ing the rule of law. {042-S08}
## What is new
What is dif­fer­ent this time, Varma ar­gued, is so­cial media, whose in­cen­tives pull ev­ery­one to­wards the ex­tremes. {042-C18}
Shah blamed so­cial media for a coun­ter­feit of knowl­edge, in which clue­less peo­ple around the din­ner table com­fort­ably mouth truths. He saw no way out “other than our striv­ing”.
Varma closed with a word for lis­ten­ers far from these coun­tries. “We all have skin in the game,” he said. “This mat­ters to all of us.”

second.label: Rich and unafraid
second.head: Money talks back
second.deck: Ajay Shah reads America’s institutions in one billionaire’s nerve

pic.caption: Jeff Bezos at the Amazon Spheres grand opening in Seattle in 2018
pic.credit: Seattle City Council from Seattle, CC BY 2.0

body: Rich peo­ple could be the most timid of all, Ajay Shah said, be­cause they have the most to lose and “you just don’t want to mess with the gov­ern­ment”. Whether they feel safe to speak up says some­thing about a coun­try. {042-S02}

In the United States, Jeff Bezos, the rich­est per­son in the coun­try, openly staked out an anti-Trump po­si­tion. He also owned the *Washington Post*, one of the news­pa­pers that ex­posed the mis­deeds of the Trump years. “Again, I say, wow,” Shah said.

Amit Varma, who counts Bezos among his he­roes, added that under him the *Post* kept run­ning anti-Amazon and anti-Bezos sto­ries. {#post} Strong in­sti­tu­tions, he said, breed val­ues that be­come part of the cul­ture.

quote.text: So in a way, rich peo­ple have hostages. They have the most to lose.

third.head: Slowly, the picture loads

pic.caption: Amit Varma on ideas that load like old photographs

body: Amit Varma re­mem­bers down­load­ing pho­to­graphs over a dial-up con­nec­tion in the 1990s, “of Samantha Fox or oth­er­wise”. First came a pix­e­lated blur. Then, grad­u­ally, the pic­ture sharp­ened into high def­i­ni­tion. {042-J07}
“Whatever the ob­jec­tives,” he said, “you get a thrill that you can see clearly.” Ideas, he said, can feel ex­actly the same way.

He too had once thought pop­ulism was some­thing like pop­u­lar, as, he said, ev­ery­body does at first. Then read­ing sup­plied what he calls frames of see­ing, and the blurry pic­ture came into focus. {042-S10}

“I just find that that’s so beau­ti­ful and mirac­u­lous,” he said, “that we can ac­tu­ally do that and make our­selves see bet­ter.” What the hosts had laid out, he said, helped him see the world bet­ter.

p2.title: The populist playbook
p2.deck: Jan-Werner Müller’s checklist, how populists keep power, and four countries where the drama is playing out

quote.text: The core claim of pop­ulism is that only some of the peo­ple are the peo­ple.

photo.caption: Jan-Werner Müller in 2021
photo.credit: Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung from Berlin, Deutschland, CC BY-SA 2.0

box.title: Seven signs, one book
box.text: Amit Varma calls Jan-Werner Müller’s *What Is Populism?* the book that taught him a lot about pop­ulism, one ev­ery­one should read. He wrote a col­umn on it long ago. It lists seven things that pop­ulists have in com­mon. {042-R01}

sections.label: Seven traits
sections.head: We the people (terms apply)
sections.caption: Müller’s seven-point checklist
body: Jan-Werner Müller, Amit Varma said, finds seven things that pop­ulists have in com­mon. First, they de­fine the peo­ple as those who sup­port them. Donald Trump, he said, once de­clared that the other peo­ple don’t mat­ter. {042-C02}
Ajay Shah added that Trump calls the press “the en­e­mies of the peo­ple”. In the same spirit, Varma said, sup­port­ers be­come pa­tri­ots and crit­ics anti-national.

The sec­ond trait is anti-elite rhetoric; the third, play­ing the vic­tim. Müller says that “ma­jori­ties act like mis­treated mi­nori­ties”, and Shah added that pop­ulists dig up some griev­ance from 500 or 50 years ago and ex­ag­ger­ate it. {042-C03}
## The use­ful enemy

The German the­o­rist Carl Schmitt, Varma said, held that what is es­sen­tial to pol­i­tics is hav­ing an enemy. With no in­vader to rally against, pop­ulists find en­e­mies within, and pose as out­siders while being hard­core in­sid­ers. Trump, he said, has been a crony cap­i­tal­ist for forty years. {042-C04}

Fourth, pop­ulist par­ties be­come per­son­al­ity cults. Fifth, the leader claims to be one of the peo­ple. Shah pointed to Trump’s photo ops eat­ing junk food. Some ham­burg­ers are tasty, Varma con­ceded, but if you say a ham­burger is good for you, “there’s a se­ri­ous kind of prob­lem with that”.
Sixth come sim­plis­tic nar­ra­tives; sev­enth, con­spir­acy the­o­ries, which grow out of populism’s own logic.
~ Varma ended the list with an old line: “Religion is the opi­ate of the masses.” Shah had a se­quel ready: “Conspiracy the­o­ries are the opi­ate of the asses.” {042-J01}

quote.text: The core claim of pop­ulism is that only some of the peo­ple are the peo­ple.

sections.label: Left and right
sections.head: Two wings, one poison
sections.caption: populism of the left and the right
body: Populism, Ajay Shah said, is not about the old clas­si­fi­ca­tion of left and right. Hitler, Mao, Lenin and Donald Trump were all pop­ulists, in very dif­fer­ent po­lit­i­cal sys­tems, and pop­ulism of the left is as toxic as pop­ulism of the right.

Amit Varma’s pre­ferred lens is an­other bi­nary: free­dom against au­thor­i­tar­i­an­ism, con­sent against co­er­cion. By that test, he said, every party in India is left on eco­nom­ics, right on so­cial is­sues and statist through­out. {042-C07}

Shah sees the cen­tral en­gine of pop­ulism as rous­ing the un­der­class to hate the elite. A move­ment stokes anger against the cul­tural, busi­ness and in­tel­lec­tual elites, com­mands the state, and then puts “the knife into the other three”. {042-C08}
## A word worth sav­ing

Shah used the word elite de­lib­er­ately, he said, “be­cause I want to tor­ment the wokes in the au­di­ence as well”. All the great truth, beauty and wealth cre­ation, he ar­gued, is done by elites. {042-J04}

Varma agreed that anti-elitism be­comes anti-knowledge, leav­ing lead­ers to take ad­vice from quacks. But elites are often com­pla­cent, en­ti­tled and con­de­scend­ing, he said, and when peo­ple vote against your val­ues, some­thing is wrong with you and your mes­sage, not with the peo­ple. {042-C09}
~ Shah traced the dan­ger back to Plato’s *Republic*, clear-eyed about democ­racy, and for­ward through Mussolini’s radio, Hitler’s ral­lies, tele­vi­sion and now so­cial media. {042-R10}

quote.text: It is con­sent and co­er­cion. That is a bi­nary.

sections.label: Holding power
sections.head: Colonise, reward, silence
sections.caption: how populists keep power
body: Winning power takes one play­book, Amit Varma said; keep­ing it takes an­other. Jan-Werner Müller de­scribes three moves that pop­ulist regimes have in com­mon. {042-C12}

First, they colonise the state, putting their own peo­ple in charge of in­de­pen­dent in­sti­tu­tions and dis­cred­it­ing the rest. It can be done by brute force or slowly. Varma reached for the para­ble of the frog in boil­ing water, then de­bunked it: the frog will at some point jump out. “But it’s a great metaphor.” {042-J12}

Second comes mass clien­telism: con­tracts, favours and pro­tec­tion from com­pe­ti­tion, es­pe­cially for­eign com­pe­ti­tion. Ajay Shah added sub­sidy pro­grammes, a crude form of po­lit­i­cal clien­telism that has be­come so nor­mal no­body no­tices.
## The Roman recipe

Shah bor­rowed a phrase from Roman his­tory: bread and cir­cus. Bread mol­li­fies peo­ple with sub­si­dies and trans­fers. The cir­cus, once glad­i­a­tors in the Colosseum, is today the noise on TV and so­cial media. {042-C14}

Third, pop­ulists shut down dis­sent in civil so­ci­ety, often start­ing with NGOs. They need not jail ev­ery­one, Varma said. Make an ex­am­ple of a cou­ple of peo­ple and the rest fall silent. {042-C13}
~ Shah saw this as part of mo­nop­o­lis­ing every or­gan­i­sa­tion in so­ci­ety. In China, he said, there is a com­mu­nist party group in­side every com­pany. {#china}

quote.text: They don’t even re­al­ize why they are silent. They may not even think they’re silent.

sections.label: United States
sections.head: When the taxman said no
sections.caption: Trump and America’s institutions
body: Ajay Shah’s first stop was the United States, where Donald Trump has taken the Republican Party far into pop­ulism. What Shah found re­mark­able was that in of­fice, Trump could not sub­vert the in­sti­tu­tions to any sig­nif­i­cant ex­tent.
Trump asked the IRS and the FBI to in­ves­ti­gate and tor­ment his ri­vals. By and large, they re­fused. In Shah’s telling, they said: “No, this is not legal. This vi­o­lates our rules.” {042-S01}
Nor could Trump stop the Democrats from rais­ing money, hir­ing ad­vi­sors, ral­ly­ing in the streets and get­ting out the vote in 2020.
## More than a fair count

That, Shah ar­gued, is what a free and fair elec­tion needs. Correct count­ing is not enough. Opposition par­ties must be able to fundraise, use a free press and or­gan­ise with­out fear of the state’s co­er­cive arms. {042-C15}
The right test, he said, is how many per­cent­age points of vote share state pres­sure on the op­po­si­tion shifts.
Even so, Shah was blown away by how small the mar­gin was: Biden just squeaked through. With the cases against Trump not played through in time, he said, Trump re­mains vi­able in 2024.
~ Amit Varma agreed. Votes, he be­lieves, are by and large counted cor­rectly in India. {#counted} What mat­ters is whether par­ties are free to cam­paign and peo­ple free to speak their minds.

quote.text: And by and large, they re­fused to do so. Can you think about that? How mar­velous is that?

portraits.caption: Donald Trump
portraits.credit: Gage Skidmore from Surprise, AZ, United States of America, CC BY-SA 2.0

sections.label: Hungary and Poland
sections.head: The star pupil comes back
sections.caption: Hungary’s slide and Poland’s return
body: Hungary, Ajay Shah said, is the coun­try of John von Neumann, and after com­mu­nism it was ex­pected to do as well as Czechoslovakia. Instead it be­came a thug­gish right-wing state, de­spite mem­ber­ship of the European Union and NATO. {042-S05}
Elections still hap­pen, but po­lice go after the op­po­si­tion, the press is gone and the Central European University was driven out. Viktor Orbán has won five times. {#orban}
## Poland’s sec­ond chance

Poland re­built quickly after 1989. Around 2005 its na­tion builders told Shah that the EU gave them “a rough work­ing draft” of what a law or an in­sti­tu­tion looks like. {042-S07} Inside the EU and NATO, Poland took off; Ukraine, out­side them, did not.

Then came ten years of the Law and Justice Party, “an al­liance be­tween farm­ers and Christians and thugs”, in Shah’s words. At the October 2023 elec­tion, Poland’s Freedom House score stood at 80 out of 100, against Hungary’s 65. {#poland80}
In that elec­tion, the cen­tre-left party led by Donald Tusk won. The task now is to undo the dam­age while re­spect­ing due process.
~ Amit Varma had a T-shirt line ready: “You are my Poland.” He imag­ined the gen­teel Shah burn­ing trucks and beat­ing peo­ple up, and hoped he too could be brought back. {042-J05}

quote.text: So you can’t just send the po­lice and grab the chief jus­tice.

sections.label: Social media
sections.head: Wired for the extremes
sections.caption: social media and the extremes
body: History may not re­peat, but it rhymes, Amit Varma said. What is new this time is the pace of tech­no­log­i­cal change and the in­cen­tives so­cial media has cre­ated. {042-J14}

Someone joins Twitter, he said, want­ing a sense of com­mu­nity, and joins an ide­o­log­i­cal tribe. Status there comes from sig­nalling, at­tack­ing the other side and can­celling in­sid­ers who are not pure enough. A vocal mi­nor­ity drags dis­course to the ex­tremes, even if the silent ma­jor­ity is not like this. {042-C18}

In 2016 he won­dered how the me­dian voter the­o­rem had bro­ken. It pre­dicted near-identical cen­trist can­di­dates, such as Jeb Bush and Hillary Clinton. Then Donald Trump won the gen­eral elec­tion.
## Groups, not peo­ple

The left is swing­ing the same way. “Wokeism be­gins where lib­er­al­ism ends,” Varma said. Liberalism is about each per­son, who con­tains mul­ti­tudes; wokeism thinks only in groups, with a ready-made story of vic­tim­hood or op­pres­sion. {042-C19}
Ajay Shah an­swered with a poet’s ques­tion, “What hap­pened to the post-war dream?”, and his own reply: so­cial media.
~ It cre­ates, Shah said, “a vul­gar fa­mil­iar­ity”, in which 140 char­ac­ters pass for knowl­edge. {042-C20} In his father’s world, peo­ple would say they had only read four books on a sub­ject.

quote.text: When I think of the in­cen­tives of so­cial media, I think the in­cen­tive ev­ery­where is to­wards the ex­tremes.
Even if the peo­ple vote in some­one who does not align with your val­ues, that doesn’t mean some­thing is wrong with the peo­ple. It means some­thing is wrong with you and your mes­sage.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A war for a soul, a murderous list, and tears in Warsaw

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah, a declared admirer, on a country at a crossroads
stories.head: Soldiers march for the judges
body: Ajay Shah put his bi­ases on the table first. He is deeply sym­pa­thetic to the project of Israel, a coun­try that, he said, came out of noth­ing and a war in 1948 and built one of the world’s great coun­tries. {#israel1948}
As a sign of its de­cency, he noted that gay peo­ple cross il­le­gally into Israel every day from neigh­bour­ing Arab coun­tries, be­cause ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity is legal there.

But after the fall of the USSR, a large wave of Jewish im­mi­grants ar­rived from Eastern Europe, most no­tably Russia, with con­ser­va­tive val­ues on re­li­gion, women and per­sonal free­dom. “So there is a war for the soul of Israel that is afoot,” Shah said. {042-S03}
It came to a head when Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s leader, tried to give the ex­ec­u­tive a veto over the se­lec­tion of judges.

People poured into the streets, and again and again the move­ment was led by peo­ple from elite mil­i­tary for­ma­tions. Their mes­sage, as Shah put it: “Look, we are sol­diers, we have given our life and our blood to pro­tect this coun­try. But we do not be­lieve that the ex­ec­u­tive branch should ride roughshod over the ju­di­cial branch.” {042-S04}

Military peo­ple, Shah said, are often the first to sign on to the de­struc­tion of in­sti­tu­tions. In Israel they cham­pi­oned the sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers, and won about 75 per cent, though not 100 per cent, of what they fought for.
~ Then came the Hamas dis­as­ter, for which Shah faults Netanyahu and the ex­ec­u­tive. The soul of Israel, he said, is up for grabs.
stories.why: In Shah’s ac­count, a democracy’s char­ac­ter rests on the val­ues its cit­i­zens carry. Change who the cit­i­zens are and the pol­i­tics can turn, and even one of the world’s great suc­cess sto­ries can slide back into the bat­tles of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma said the bat­tle for Israel’s soul was news to him, and some­thing he would be fol­low­ing.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the war for Israel’s soul

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how Poland lost its elite
stories.head: Forty thousand names
body: Poland, Ajay Shah said, was sav­aged for cen­turies by mon­strous neigh­bours on ei­ther side. On 1 September 1939 Nazi Germany in­vaded; on 16 September, the Russians fol­lowed. {#invaded}

After the Second World War the Russians swal­lowed Poland and in­stalled a com­mu­nist party. Stalin took care to draw up a list of 40,000 peo­ple of the Polish elite, and they were mur­dered. {042-S06}

Shah asked lis­ten­ers to pause and think of any coun­try they love. “Imagine a care­fully made list of the forty thou­sand peo­ple who make up the in­tel­lec­tual and the busi­ness and the cul­tural elite of the coun­try. And imag­ine that they get mur­dered.”
~ That is where mod­ern Poland began, he said. Yet it was among the first to build an anti-communist move­ment, with Lech Walesa or­gan­is­ing its port work­ers.
stories.why: Culture is trans­mit­ted by peo­ple, Shah said, and those 40,000 were dis­pro­por­tion­ately im­por­tant car­ri­ers of knowl­edge, val­ues and norms. Losing them is like de­stroy­ing the foun­da­tions of a coun­try, and re­build­ing takes gen­er­a­tions.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on history and the art of travel
stories.head: Tears on the tourist trail
body: For peo­ple who read his­tory, Ajay Shah said, there are few things more mov­ing than vis­it­ing Poland. He once spent three days vis­it­ing sites in Warsaw, “just weep­ing like a baby”. {#warsaw}
Amit Varma, think­ing aloud, said the story of any place is also a story of human civil­i­sa­tion, and Poland stood at the cen­tre of so much of the last century’s tur­moil.

A tourist who ar­rives with­out any im­pres­sions will see build­ings and streets and no­tice the weather, he said. But the deeper you go, the more ev­ery­thing sud­denly has mean­ing and sig­nif­i­cance.

~ Shah had the last word. “The magic of travel is the child of learn­ing cul­ture, learn­ing his­tory. Then travel comes alive.” Otherwise, he said, you are just sight­see­ing, and might as well go to the beach in Goa. {042-S09}
stories.why: Knowing a place’s his­tory turns sight­see­ing into an en­counter with human civil­i­sa­tion. For both hosts, the read­ing done be­fore a jour­ney is what gives the build­ings and streets of a city their mean­ing.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on three days in Warsaw

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why the hosts stayed out of a war
stories.head: Nuance draws fire from both sides
body: After the Hamas at­tacks and Israel’s re­tal­i­a­tion, lis­ten­ers asked the hosts to dis­cuss the war. They de­clined, Amit Varma said, be­cause they did not have enough knowl­edge of some­thing so com­plex.

He still set out what he called a nu­anced po­si­tion. He is against Hamas, which he called evil, and against the Israeli state as it cur­rently is. {#position} He cares deeply for the Palestinian peo­ple and sym­pa­thises with the Israeli peo­ple.

Even that, he said, gets you at­tacked, be­cause ev­ery­thing is black and white. “If you speak against Israel, it is as­sumed you are anti-Semitic, which is daft. If you speak against Hamas, it is as­sumed that you’re against the Palestinian peo­ple, which is daft.” {042-S11}
~ Hamas, in his opin­ion, is the worst thing that hap­pened to Palestine. Beyond that, he said, he knew too lit­tle to com­ment.

quote.text: I am with the peo­ple on both sides.

overheard.text: Please cor­rect me if you think I’m right.
overheard.who: Ajay Shah, after Amit warned listeners would correct him even when right

quiz.q: Which German theorist said that what is essential to politics is having an enemy?
quiz.a: Carl Schmitt, whose idea Amit Varma used to ex­plain populists’ in­ter­nal en­e­mies.

quiz.q: Which two agencies did Donald Trump ask to torment his rivals, and how did they respond?
quiz.a: The IRS and the FBI, and by and large they re­fused.

quiz.q: How many of Poland’s elite were on the list Stalin had drawn up?
quiz.a: Forty thou­sand peo­ple, who were mur­dered, de­stroy­ing the foun­da­tions of the coun­try.

quiz.q: What Freedom House score did Hungary get, though Ajay Shah says its democracy has been destroyed?
quiz.a: 65 out of 100, which he says is con­sis­tent with sus­tained loss of democ­racy.

quiz.q: Which Roman phrase did Ajay Shah use for the machinery of the modern populist?
quiz.a: Bread and cir­cus: sub­si­dies to pla­cate peo­ple, spec­ta­cle to stop them think­ing.

quiz.q: Ajay Shah spent his life worrying about *1984*. Which novel does he think we stumbled into?
quiz.a: William Golding’s *Lord of the Flies*, where peo­ple bully and tor­ment each other.

glossary.def: Politics claim­ing that only some of the peo­ple are the peo­ple
Doling out favours, con­tracts and sub­si­dies to re­ward loyal groups
Voters busy earn­ing a liv­ing have no time to get in­formed
Punish a few, and ev­ery­one else starts to cen­sor them­selves
Rival can­di­dates in a gen­eral elec­tion end up near the cen­tre
One who needs pic­tures; give him the il­lus­trated *On Tyranny*

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 42. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Joseph Stalin (Ivan Shagin, public domain); Jan-Werner Müller (Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung from Berlin, Deutschland, CC BY-SA 2.0); Jeff Bezos (Seattle City Council from Seattle, CC BY 2.0); Carl Schmitt (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Plato (Marie-Lan Nguyen, CC BY 2.5); Donald Trump Jr. (Gage Skidmore from Surprise, AZ, United States of America, CC BY-SA 2.0); Timothy Snyder (Jindřich Nosek (NoJin), CC BY 4.0); William Golding (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 nl).

shelf.title: What Is Populism?
shelf.creator: Jan-Werner Müller
shelf.why: The book that taught Amit most of what he knows about pop­ulism: it re­places the naive ‘pop­ulism = popular’ with a pre­cise check­list for spot­ting pop­ulists any­where.

shelf.title: Why Both Modi and Trump Are Textbook Populists
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit ap­plies Müller’s frame­work to two con­tem­po­rary lead­ers and shows how slo­gan-sized sto­ries crowd out com­plex truths.

shelf.title: Facts Don’t Matter, Stories Do
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It ar­gues that Trump won a fol­low­ing by of­fer­ing sim­ple sto­ries: jobs shipped over­seas, im­mi­grants tak­ing jobs.

shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: Amit says it will teach you so much about pol­i­tics and calls it a mas­ter­piece that feels like ‘the fu­ture writ­ten in the past.’

shelf.title: Animal Farm
shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: Amit calls both nov­els mas­ter­pieces that teach you a great deal about pol­i­tics and the world.

shelf.title: Essays
shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: Orwell’s non­fic­tion, which Amit prefers to the nov­els: a chrono­log­i­cal look at Orwell the thinker, who banged out three or four bril­liant col­umns a week.

shelf.title: Lord of the Flies
shelf.creator: William Golding
shelf.why: Ajay spent his life wor­ry­ing about 1984, but feels we have stum­bled into Lord of the Flies in­stead.

shelf.title: On Tyranny
shelf.creator: Timothy Snyder
shelf.why: Ajay thinks it is im­por­tant enough to rec­om­mend a sec­ond time in an episode about the pop­ulist threat to democ­racy.

shelf.title: On Tyranny (graphic edition)
shelf.creator: Timothy Snyder and Nora Krug
shelf.why: An il­lus­trated ver­sion for read­ers who need pic­tures.

shelf.title: Republic
shelf.creator: Plato
shelf.why: Plato was clear-eyed about democracy’s weak­nesses long be­fore radio, ral­lies, TV and so­cial media made it easy to blast sim­plis­tic mes­sages to the masses.

shelf.title: Private Truths, Public Lies
shelf.creator: Timur Kuran
shelf.why: Kuran’s the­ory of pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion and pref­er­ence cas­cades: regimes look unan­i­mously sup­ported until peo­ple dis­cover that oth­ers se­cretly dis­agree too.

shelf.title: Freedom House
shelf.creator: Freedom House
shelf.why: Freedom House’s democ­racy rank­ings, from Norway at the top to North Korea at the bot­tom: a de­cent, easy-to-use mea­sure.

shelf.title: V-Dem
shelf.why: Ajay thinks V-Dem is in many ways the bet­ter mea­sure of democ­racy, though more work to use.

shelf.title: Beauty and the Beast (1991)
shelf.creator: Walt Disney
shelf.why: Its scene of the male char­ac­ter flip­ping through Belle’s book, com­plain­ing it has no pic­tures, and Belle re­ply­ing that some peo­ple can use their imag­i­na­tion.

shelf.title: Words
shelf.creator: Bee Gees
shelf.why: ‘It’s only words and words are all we have’ cap­tures the episode’s open­ing point: get­ting the tech­ni­cal mean­ing of words right is the foun­da­tion of clear think­ing.

shelf.title: The India Uncut Newsletter
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s news­let­ter, where he thinks through ideas like vir­tu­ous and vi­cious cy­cles be­fore they reach the show.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world prob­lems: jour­nal-based pro­mo­tion and de­part­men­tal in­cen­tives nar­row every dis­ci­pline, fil­ter out cre­ative mav­er­icks and leave aca­demics writ­ing for each other.

shelf.title: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on the power sec­tor: solar, wind, stor­age and time-of-day pric­ing, why elec­tric­ity prices must be al­lowed to move, and why fix­ing Indian power is a 25-year jour­ney that Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing de­pends on.

laughs.text: Amit, after his point on con­spir­acy the­o­ries: ‘Religion is the opi­ate of the masses.’ Ajay: ‘Conspiracy the­o­ries are the opi­ate of the asses.’

Amit the writ­ing teacher po­lices Ajay’s mixed metaphors all episode. First: ‘You can pour salt on a wound and you can pour oil on a fire. Why would you pour salt on a fire, Ajay Shah?’ (‘My mis­take.’). Then ‘a black eye in the heart of Europe. What is this?’ Finally, ‘the spinal cord of the foun­da­tion. My brain is going to hell,’ and the two set­tle on call­ing it ‘the struc­tural en­gi­neer­ing of this episode.’

On Trump’s junk-food photo ops, Amit: ‘I can com­pletely un­der­stand why some­one says a ham­burger is tasty. Yes, some ham­burg­ers are tasty. But if you tell me a ham­burger is good for you, you know, there’s a se­ri­ous kind of prob­lem with that.’
Ajay, de­lib­er­ately: ‘Gentle reader, you will be notic­ing my ex­plicit use of the word elite, be­cause I want to tor­ment the wokes in the au­di­ence as well.’

When Ajay says even star pupil Poland col­lapsed into pop­ulism, Amit coins a ‘T-shirt line’: ‘You are my Poland.’ He imag­ines the gen­teel, nu­anced Ajay sud­denly ‘burn­ing trucks and beat­ing peo­ple up,’ with hope that he too can be brought back.
Amit’s 90s nos­tal­gia: down­load­ing pho­to­graphs over dial-up ‘of Samantha Fox or otherwise’ and watch­ing them sharpen from pix­els. ‘Whatever the ob­jec­tives, you get a thrill.’

Ajay sets up his rec­om­men­da­tion with Beauty and the Beast: the male char­ac­ter (‘con­ser­va­tive, toxic mas­culin­ity, all that stuff’) flips through Belle’s book and com­plains there are no pic­tures. Hence the il­lus­trated On Tyranny, ‘that you should give every WhatsApp uncle in your life.’

The episode opens with Amit hold­ing a prop: ‘an an­cient man­u­script that we have found, which looks like a leaf’ cov­ered in ‘mys­te­ri­ous words in a mys­te­ri­ous lan­guage.’ Later, when Ajay says events in far­away coun­tries mat­ter to all of us, Amit brings the leaf back with a play on ‘for whom the bell tolls’: ‘not for whom the leaf turns, the leaf turns for thee.’
Ajay piv­ots to defin­ing pop­ulism with the Bee Gees’ ‘Words’: ‘It’s only words and words are all we have.’ Amit: ‘I never thought you’re gonna quote the Bee Gees at me, but well done.’

Asked what is driv­ing today’s po­lar­i­sa­tion, Ajay quotes ‘a poet’: ‘some­body shout, some­body scream, what hap­pened to the post-war dream?’ His an­swer to the lyric’s ques­tion is so­cial media.

The frog in slowly boil­ing water: Amit uses the para­ble for grad­ual in­sti­tu­tional cap­ture, then de­bunks it. ‘It’s a myth. If you heat the water and a frog is in it, the frog will at some point jump out. But it’s a great metaphor.’
‘History may not re­peat, but it rhymes.’ Amit in­vokes the line to ask what is gen­uinely new this time, and an­swers: the pace of tech­nol­ogy and the in­cen­tives of so­cial media.
